explanations.answer: Pass it down generation after generation
explanations.explanation: Joel says it plainly: “Tell it to your children; let your children tell it to their children, and their children to the next generation.” That's a story with a long road ahead of it. I can barely get a cookie recipe through one retelling before somebody swaps out the sprinkles. He's speaking to the elders and everyone in the land, so the whole land is in on this.

explanations.answer: Carve it into the city gate
explanations.explanation: Joel never says a word about carving anything. He says to tell it, and to keep telling it, from children to their children. A city gate is a lot of chiseling anyway, and all I do is stamp cookies. This story travels by mouth.

Joel's call goes out to the elders and to “all who dwell in the land.” Then he says to tell it to your children, and for them to tell theirs. That's not a secret for a few people in one room. It's a story headed far past the priests.

Joel lines them up one by one. What the devouring locust left, the swarming locust ate. What the swarming locust left, the young locust ate, and what the young locust left, the destroying locust ate. It's like four people going through a cookie box in a row, and the last one is down on his knees hunting crumbs.

The text says just the opposite. Joel says, “What the devouring locust has left, the swarming locust has eaten…” and keeps going down the line. Each kind eats what the kind before it left behind. That's four rounds, and nobody gets a second helping.

explanations.answer: The sweet wine is cut off from them
explanations.explanation: Joel says to “wail, all you drinkers of wine, because of the sweet wine, for it has been cut off from your mouth.” The text names the loss and nothing else. I get a little weepy myself when the last cookie on the plate disappears, so I can see how it feels. This was a whole supply gone.

explanations.answer: Their wine jars have been smashed
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions any smashed jars. Joel says the sweet wine “has been cut off from your mouth.” That's the reason he gives for the wailing. The wine is simply gone.

explanations.answer: The king has banned all their feasts
explanations.explanation: No king shows up anywhere in these verses, and nobody bans a feast. Joel's reason is right there in verse 5: the sweet wine has been cut off from their mouths. He doesn't say who or what ordered it.

Joel says this nation “has laid waste My grapevine and splintered My fig tree.” Then it strips off the bark and throws it away, and the branches turn white. Splintered means broken into pieces, friend. Nobody was gentle about it.

Joel never says the tree gets pulled out of the ground. He says the nation “splintered My fig tree.” It strips off the bark and throws it away, and the branches turn white. The tree is broken up, not pulled up.

Pruning is when a gardener snips a little to help a tree along, and this nation didn't bring tiny scissors. Joel says it laid waste the grapevine and splintered the fig tree. It also strips off the bark and throws it away. That's the opposite of a careful trim.

Joel says, “Grain and drink offerings have been cut off from the house of the LORD.” The loss in the fields reaches all the way to the house of the LORD. He says the same thing again in verse 13, so he clearly wants it to land. When the grain goes, so do the offerings.

Incense isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage. Joel names the grain and drink offerings as the ones cut off from the house of the LORD. Those are the two he keeps coming back to. Verse 13 repeats them.

No lamb shows up in these verses. What Joel says is cut off from the house of the LORD is “grain and drink offerings.” He mentions them in verse 9 and again in verse 13. The loss from the field walks right through the temple door.

Joel says the opposite. He says “the priests are in mourning, those who minister before the LORD.” Nobody in the house of the LORD is celebrating, because the grain and drink offerings have been cut off. It's a sad room.

That's right, and it's a sad picture. Joel says, “the priests are in mourning, those who minister before the LORD.” The grain and drink offerings have been cut off from the house of the LORD. I think this is one of the quieter, heavier parts of the passage.

Joel says, “Be dismayed, O farmers, wail, O vinedressers, over the wheat and barley…” Those are the people who worked the ground and the vines, so they're the ones who feel it first. The harvest of the field has perished. That's a whole season of work, gone.

Joel does talk about cattle, herds and flocks later in the passage, but that's not who he calls out in verse 11. Here he says, “Be dismayed, O farmers, wail, O vinedressers…” They're the ones with the wheat and barley. The harvest of the field has perished.

No merchants or traders show up in these verses. Joel calls on the farmers and the vinedressers to wail over the wheat and barley. The harvest of the field has perished. That's about as close to the ground as a loss can get.

Joel says, “Surely the joy of mankind has dried up.” That's after he names the grapevine, the fig, the pomegranate, the palm and the apple, all withered. Take away the food and the festivals, and the smiles go with them. I've seen what happens to a bakery with no flour. Nobody's laughing.
Joel doesn't say wisdom dried up. His words are “Surely the joy of mankind has dried up.” He's looking at an orchard where every tree has withered. What's gone is joy.
Fear isn't what Joel says has dried up. He says, “Surely the joy of mankind has dried up.” That's his summary after he walks through every withered tree in the orchard. The loss he names is joy.

Joel says, “Come, spend the night in sackcloth, O ministers of my God…” So it's one night, start to finish. He's speaking to the ministers of the altar. The grain and drink offerings are withheld from the house of their God.
Joel never gives a number of days. He says, “Come, spend the night in sackcloth, O ministers of my God.” That's the night, not the week. It's a long night all the same.

Joel doesn't say anything about waiting for a harvest. He tells the ministers to “spend the night in sackcloth.” That's the stretch of time he names. The reason he gives is that the grain and drink offerings are withheld from the house of their God.

Joel says, “Gather the elders and all the residents of the land to the house of the LORD your God.” He called out to the elders back in verse 2, so they're in this from the start. And then everybody else comes too. That's the whole community in one place.
Soldiers never show up in this passage. Joel says to gather “the elders and all the residents of the land.” The call goes out to everyone who lives there. The place is the house of the LORD.
Joel doesn't mention nobles. He says to gather the elders and all the residents of the land to the house of the LORD. It's the elders first, and then everybody. No special seating.

Joel says to gather them at the house of the LORD “and cry out to the LORD.” That's the instruction once everyone is in the room. No plan, no speeches, just crying out to Him. Sometimes that's the whole bake.

Joel doesn't call for a great sacrifice here. He says the grain and drink offerings are withheld from the house of their God (verse 13), and for this gathering he says to “cry out to the LORD.” That's his instruction.
Nobody is picking a new leader in these verses. Joel says to gather the elders and all the residents of the land, and then “cry out to the LORD.” That's the whole assignment.

Joel says the opposite: “For the Day of the LORD is near.” He doesn't call it far off. He also says it “will come as destruction from the Almighty.” I think this is a heavy line, and it's worth sitting quietly with.

That's right. Joel says, “Alas for the day! For the Day of the LORD is near, and it will come as destruction from the Almighty.” He says near, not far off. It's a heavy moment, and Joel doesn't soften it.

Joel says, “…it will come as destruction from the Almighty.” That's a heavy word and there's no joke to make about it. He says it right after “Alas for the day!” I think this is one of the most serious lines in the passage.
Thunder isn't in this verse. Joel says the Day of the LORD “will come as destruction from the Almighty.” It's a heavy line, and I think it deserves a quiet moment.
Darkness isn't a word in this passage. Joel says the Day of the LORD “will come as destruction from the Almighty.” That's the word he picks. It's a heavy one, so I'll just leave it there.

Joel says, “…the storehouses are in ruins; the granaries are broken down, for the grain has withered away.” A granary is where the grain is kept, and the grain is gone. A storage building with nothing to store is a pretty sad building. Think of an empty cookie jar, only a whole lot bigger.
No earthquake is mentioned here. Joel says the granaries are broken down “for the grain has withered away.” That's the reason the text gives. The grain is gone, and the granaries are broken down.

explanations.answer: A flood has washed them out
explanations.explanation: There's no flood in these verses. In fact, Joel says the streams of water have dried up (verse 20). The granaries are broken down “for the grain has withered away.” That's the reason he gives.

Joel says, “How the cattle groan! The herds wander in confusion because they have no pasture.” The text gives that as the reason. A herd with nothing to graze on has nowhere to settle. Even the flocks of sheep are suffering.
Joel doesn't mention raiders anywhere in these verses. He says the herds “wander in confusion because they have no pasture.” That's the reason the text gives. Even the flocks of sheep are suffering.
There's no storm in this passage. Joel says the herds “wander in confusion because they have no pasture.” That's his reason. The cattle groan and the sheep suffer too.

The prayer says, “To You, O LORD, I call, for fire has consumed the open pastures and flames have scorched all the trees of the field.” That's fire and flames, both in one verse. It's a hard picture, and the prayer takes it straight to the LORD. That's where it goes.
Hail isn't mentioned in these verses. The prayer says, “…fire has consumed the open pastures and flames have scorched all the trees of the field.” It's a heavy picture, and it all goes to the LORD.

Frost doesn't show up anywhere in this passage. The prayer says, “…fire has consumed the open pastures and flames have scorched all the trees of the field.” It's a heavy moment, and the prayer is lifted up to the LORD.

The prayer says, “Even the beasts of the field pant for You, for the streams of water have dried up…” So the prayer isn't only from people. The animals are in the same dry place, reaching toward Him. I think that's one of the most tender lines in the whole passage.
Birds aren't named in this prayer. It says, “Even the beasts of the field pant for You, for the streams of water have dried up…” The panting belongs to the beasts of the field. The streams are dry.

Fish don't show up anywhere in this passage. The prayer says, “Even the beasts of the field pant for You…” and it gives the reason: the streams of water have dried up. It's the animals on dry ground that are panting.
